> 善建者不拔，善抱者不脫，子孫以祭祀不輟.

Chapter 53 looked at the age: high steps, overgrown fields, empty granaries. Chapter 54 gives the opposite answer — don't build outward, establish inward.

Four characters carry it, and all four are more physical than the modern reading.

## 建 is to stand a line up with a pen

建: 立朝律也 — to establish the law of the court. The character has 聿 (the writing brush) in it: a line drawn and made to stand.

So 善建者 is not a good builder of walls. It is the one who draws a line that stands.

拔: 擢也 — to pull up, to pluck out from above. 不拔: it cannot be pulled up.

A wall can be pulled down because it is a thing. A law that has been drawn into how people act is not a thing; there is nothing to grip.

## 抱 is to cradle in the lapel

抱's old form is 袌, built on 衣 — clothing. It is to hold something in the fold of the garment, not lock the arms around it.

That is why 不脫: what is held in the lapel does not slip free, because it is being carried by the body that moves, not gripped by arms that tire.

## 輟 is a cart missing a segment

輟: 車小缺復合者也 — a cart that is missing a short stretch and rejoins.

So 子孫以祭祀不輟 is not "the sacrifices never cease" in a solemn sense. It is: not one segment has been dropped. The line runs continuously, and continuity is the whole achievement.

## 修之於身

Five 修's: 身, 家, 鄉, 邦, 天下. And each is given a different 德: 真, 餘, 長, 豐, 普.

真 — real, not apparent. 餘 — surplus, more than the household needs. 長 — lasting. 豐 — abundant. 普 — everywhere.

The order is outward, and the quality changes with the scope, but the origin does not move: it starts at the body.

## 以身觀身

Five 觀's, and the wording is exact: use a body to observe bodies; use a household to observe households.

觀 is the character with the stork on it — the standing bird. It is to look from a settled position, the same 觀 as chapter 1's 觀其妙.

The method is not comparison. It is: the thing you are observing is observed from inside the same kind of thing. You know a household by being in one, not by counting households.

## 吾何以知天下然哉？以此

How do I know the world is like this? By this.

以此 — the same closing as chapter 21. Not by data, not by report. By the one instrument that is not an aperture: the thing itself, observed from within its own kind.

## Why this follows 53

53 diagnosed a state whose surface was finished and whose base was empty.
54 says the base is built at the scale of a body, and only then extends.

Which is an uncomfortable order for anyone who wants to fix the world first. The chapter's claim is that the world is legible only from a position that has been established — otherwise you are observing through a frame and calling it the world.

## A test

Take one thing you have built that you would not have to defend if it were attacked. Then ask at what scale it was built. Almost always: at the scale of your own daily practice, not at the scale of the announcement about it.
